title: How to Fix Squeaky Wooden Stairs (From Above or Below)
question: My wooden stairs squeak loudly every time someone walks on them — how do I stop the squeaking for good?
summary: Stairs squeak because a tread has worked loose from the riser or the stringer underneath, so wood rubs against wood (or against a loosened nail) when you put weight on it. The mistake most people make is hammering in another nail from the top — nails work loose again and pounding can widen the gap. The durable fix is screws driven into the actual framing (riser or stringer) plus glue, and the strongest, invisible fix is done from underneath the stairs if you can reach it.

commonCauses.cause: Tread has pulled loose from the riser at the front edge
commonCauses.quickCheck: Press or step on the front edge of the tread right where it meets the riser; if it dips or squeaks there, that joint is loose.

commonCauses.cause: Tread has loosened from a stringer (the sawtooth support under the steps)
commonCauses.quickCheck: Step on the ends of the tread over each stringer and listen; if accessible, have someone walk while you watch from below for the tread flexing on the stringer.

commonCauses.cause: Old nails have popped or no longer grip, so the nail shank rubs the wood
commonCauses.quickCheck: Look for nail heads standing proud of the tread, or a squeak that briefly stops right after you step (the nail re-seating).

commonCauses.cause: Glue blocks under the stairs dried out and fell off
commonCauses.quickCheck: Look under the staircase for loose triangular wood blocks lying at the base of the risers where they should be glued in the corners.

commonCauses.cause: Seasonal wood shrinkage opened small gaps, leaving wood rubbing on wood
commonCauses.quickCheck: Note whether the squeaks come and go with the seasons — worse in dry winter months points to shrinkage gaps rather than a truly loose tread.

fixes: Pinpoint the squeak: have a helper step slowly on each tread — front edge, middle, back, and both ends — while you listen and watch. Mark each squeak spot with painter's tape and note whether it is at the front (tread meets riser) or under the tread (tread meets stringer).

Decide your access. If the underside of the stairs is open (a basement or a closet under the stairs), fix from below — it is stronger and leaves no marks on the steps. If the underside is closed off, fix from above.

From below, add or re-seat glue blocks: at each corner where the underside of a tread meets its riser, run a bead of wood glue or construction adhesive, press a triangular hardwood block into the inside corner, and screw it into both the tread and the riser with 1-1/4 to 1-1/2 inch screws — long enough to grip both pieces but short enough that they never break through the tread's top face or the riser's front face. Space blocks every 6 to 8 inches and replace any that had fallen off.

From below, screw the tread down to the stringer: where the tread has lifted off a stringer, predrill and drive wood screws up through the stringer into the underside of the tread. Size the screw carefully — it must first pass through the full thickness of the stringer seat (often about 1-1/2 inch on a sawtooth stringer) before it reaches the tread, so it commonly needs to be a 2 to 2-1/2 inch screw, yet it must stop about 1/4 inch below the top face of the tread so it never pokes through. Measure stringer-plus-tread and size to that. (If you ever drive straight into a bare tread's underside with no framing in between, use a screw shorter than the tread is thick.)

From below, shim any open gap: coat a wood shim with glue, tap it gently into the gap between tread and stringer until snug, then trim it flush with a utility knife. Do not force it — hard hammering lifts the tread and makes the squeak worse.

From above, find the framing first: your screws must land in the riser directly below the tread's front edge, or in a stringer (one at each end, sometimes one in the middle). Screwing into the tread alone will not hold. A stud finder helps locate a hidden middle stringer.

From above on bare wood, predrill and countersink, then drive two 2 to 2-1/2 inch trim-head or deck screws through the tread down into the riser or stringer to pull the tread tight. Angling a pair slightly toward each other adds grip.
Hide the screws: set the heads just below the surface, fill with stain-matched wood filler, sand smooth, and touch up the finish.

From above on carpeted stairs, use a squeak-repair kit (such as Squeeeeek No More / Counter-Snap): drive the special breakaway screw through the carpet into the stringer or riser using the kit's depth fixture, then rock the tool to snap the head off below the carpet so it disappears.

For a minor wood-on-wood squeak you cannot screw, puff powdered graphite or sprinkle talcum powder into the joint between the tread and riser to cut the friction — a quick touch-up, not a fix for a genuinely loose tread.

Retest: have your helper walk the whole flight again to confirm it is silent before you fill, sand, or refinish. If a step still moves or the entire flight flexes, that is structural — stop and call a carpenter.
diyVsPro: Fixing a squeaky tread is a beginner-friendly DIY job — most cases are solved with a few screws, glue, and shims for under $40. Stop and call a licensed carpenter or contractor if a tread is cracked, split, or soft/rotted; if the staircase feels wobbly or the whole flight flexes underfoot (that is loose framing, not just a squeak); if treads are pulling away from the wall or the stringers have cracked; or on an old home where you are unsure what is structural. A persistent squeak that returns after a proper screw-and-glue repair also points to a deeper framing problem worth a professional look.
typicalCostUSD: DIY: about $10–40 for screws, adhesive, shims, and wood filler, or roughly $20–25 for a carpeted-stair squeak kit. Pro: about $100–300 for a handyman or carpenter visit to fix a few treads, more if several steps need work or an above-the-tread repair requires refinishing.
timeEstimate: 30 minutes to 2 hours for a few squeaky steps; a half day for a full flight, plus drying and finishing time.
safetyNote: The main hazard is falling: block off the staircase and keep the steps and your work path clear of tools while you work, and never leave loose treads or shims sticking up for someone to trip on. Wear safety glasses when drilling and driving screws — heads can snap and fly, especially the breakaway screws in carpet squeak kits. Predrill hardwood treads so they do not split, and tap shims gently rather than hammering hard, which can crack or lift a tread. When driving screws blind (up through a stringer from below, or through carpet), size them so the tip stops about 1/4 inch short of the tread's top face — an over-long screw can break through the walking surface and become a foot hazard. A squeak itself is cosmetic, but if a tread is cracked or rotted, the stairs feel wobbly, or the whole flight moves or pulls away from the wall, that is a structural issue — stop and hire a licensed carpenter. No electrical or gas work is involved in this repair.
toolsParts: Trim-head or deck screws, 2 to 2-1/2 inch (from above; also for driving up through a stringer from below)
Triangular hardwood glue blocks (or scrap wood to cut your own)
Carpeted-stair squeak kit (e.g., Squeeeeek No More / Counter-Snap)
Stud finder (to locate a hidden middle stringer)
